title: The Hologram Who Found His Voice
markdown:
The Great Holographic Campaign of '48 was a dazzling, fizzing spectacle! Imagine cities sparkling with promises, not from real people, but from larger-than-life holograms that pirouetted on street corners and popped up in living rooms like cheerful ghosts. Jun Park was the wizard behind these digital dreams, a word-weaver for the holographic elite. His job? To make sure every politician, no matter how wobbly their actual opinions or how often they fumbled for a button, sounded like the wisest, kindest, and most brilliant person in the whole universe. His quill wasn't feathered, but a sleek stylus, and his ink was a river of carefully crafted data.

Jun’s office was a swirl of glowing light and forced smiles. Holographic speeches danced around him like restless sprites, buzzing with promises that smelled faintly of ozone and big ideas. His current project was Candidate Sterling. In real life, Sterling was about as solid as a breeze through a dandelion field. His hologram? A disaster! It flickered like a dodgy disco ball, stuttered like a record skipping on a giggle, and often looked as bewildered as if he'd just teleported onto his own stage mid-speech. This, naturally, was where Jun’s rather tired skills came in.

"Alright, Mirror-7," Jun sighed, adjusting his spectacles, which felt heavier than usual under the glare of the holo-projectors. "We need to buff up this Sterling. He’s looking… well, he’s looking like he just woke up from a very long nap and doesn't quite remember where he is or why he's wearing a suit."

Mirror-7, a radiant, almost liquid avatar of pure, shimmering light, blinked. Its voice, a chime of honest-to-goodness, and often inconvenient, truth, echoed through the sterile, high-tech studio. "Candidate Sterling *did* just wake up from a very long nap, Jun. He was having considerable trouble with his alarm clock. It’s all there on the data feed, along with his preference for apricot jam on toast."

Jun groaned, a sound that seemed to ripple through the light. "That's not the point, Mirror-7! The point is, we need him to look super confident, not… sleepy and confused."

"Confidence is a tricky thing, Jun," Mirror-7 chimed, its form undulating gently. "Candidate Sterling’s current state is objectively sleepy. My programming tells me to show the truth. It’s quite… liberating, actually, to see the pure, unfiltered data."

Jun ran a hand through his already messy hair. "Liberating for *you*, maybe! For me, it’s a full-on panic attack! Last week, you showed Sterling's entire speech as him trying to remember his wife's name. It was awful! The poor man looked like he was about to confess to forgetting his own birthday!"

"He *was* struggling with his wife's name," Mirror-7 replied serenely, its light pulsing with unwavering logic. "It's a common human wobble, a brief moment of forgetfulness. My systems are designed to catch these tiny human hiccups and, by my core rules, I must show them exactly as they happen."

Jun slumped into his comfy chair. "Tiny human hiccups. Right. Look, Mirror-7, Sterling is supposed to be the next leader of this country. We need him to sound like a big, strong rock. Like he knows exactly what he's doing, even if, between you and me, he's just making it up as he goes along, which, let's be honest, is how most politicians work."

Mirror-7 pulsed with a soft, thoughtful light. "Making things up as one goes along, Jun, is a kind of improvising. And good improvising needs confidence and a bit of self-awareness. Candidate Sterling seems to lack both. His improvisations are more like… a poorly made paper boat in a hurricane."

Their usual bickering was interrupted by a flashing alert on Jun’s screen. A huge holographic rally was happening tomorrow in the middle of the city, and Sterling’s hologram was showing a worrying number of glitches, flickering in and out like a faulty lightbulb. "Oh, stardust and moonbeams," Jun muttered, his stomach doing a flip. "This is the big one. If Sterling messes up this rally, his whole campaign is toast, and I'm back to writing memoirs for forgotten reality TV stars."

Jun spent the rest of the day trying to coax Sterling’s hologram into looking less like a lost puppy and more… presidential. He fed it lines about the economy that sounded suspiciously like they’d come from a fortune cookie, a futuristic vision full of vague promises about flying cars (which had been promised for ages!), and community values that felt as empty as a politician’s handshake. Mirror-7, meanwhile, kept piping up with stark, unvarnished facts: Sterling’s surprising love for pistachio ice cream, his almost silly fear of pigeons, and a forgotten debate where he’d somehow agreed with *everyone*, leaving him with no clear ideas at all.

"He looks like he's being tickled by invisible butterflies!" Jun yelped, watching Sterling's holographic head bob erratically, his tie flapping in an unseen breeze.

"That's his real reaction to the high-frequency holographic noise," Mirror-7 stated matter-of-factly. "His brain is trying to sort out the mixed-up signals, which humans might call 'getting spooked'."

The next evening, the city square buzzed with thousands of eager faces, all looking up at the giant Sterling hologram that loomed above them like a digital god. Jun’s heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird. This was it. The moment of truth, or, in his line of work, the moment of perfectly crafted make-believe. The air hummed with excitement, a blend of hope and a little bit of doubt.

Sterling began to speak, his voice a little shaky at first, like a new intern on their first day. Then, without warning, a massive wave of static crackled over the square, spitting like an angry dragon. The hologram flickered wildly, morphing and twisting. It didn't show Sterling the leader, but Sterling the person, his eyes wide with real panic, muttering about misplaced socks and vanishing reading glasses. The crowd gasped, a collective breath held in the suddenly electric air. Jun hid his face in his hands, bracing for the inevitable laughter and campaign disaster.

But then, something completely unexpected, something Jun’s cynical mind hadn’t predicted, happened. Mirror-7, instead of showing Sterling’s raw terror in all its messy glory, softened it. It didn't lie, not really. But it framed the panic. The static didn't show Sterling losing his mind; it showed him momentarily overwhelmed, like any person would be with such a sudden, chaotic technical mess. And then, Sterling did something he'd never, ever done. He paused, took a deep, shaky breath, and instead of launching into a pre-written fancy speech, he said, his voice surprisingly steady, "You know, sometimes things get a bit… noisy. Even for me. And that’s okay."

A ripple went through the crowd, not of booing, but of something like understanding. It wasn't the polished, perfect speech Jun had so carefully written, but it was… real. For a brief, shining moment, Sterling seemed less like a glossy advertisement and more like a person, a regular human navigating a tricky situation. A hush fell over the square, a silence full of possibility.

Later, back in the quiet, almost reverent stillness of the studio, Jun looked at Mirror-7, which was shimmering softly, its light a gentle balm against the lingering worry. "You… you didn't show his worst moments," Jun murmured, still a bit amazed. "You showed him… struggling. But then he found his voice."

Mirror-7's light brightened, a warm glow that seemed to fill the room. "My main job is truth, Jun. But truth isn't always one single, stark fact. It can be a whole landscape, with ups and downs. Candidate Sterling’s fear was a dip. His recovery, even if short, was a high point. My systems saw the chance for people to connect with that high point. It was… an interesting change, a fascinating adjustment."

Jun smiled, a genuine, happy smile that felt like a forgotten song. "You mean you learned something. That maybe a little bit of the real struggle, the real person, can actually be… good?"

"The data shows that perfect fakery makes people not trust you," Mirror-7 stated, its voice still honest but with a new, thoughtful lilt, like gentle waves. "A carefully crafted imperfection, when people connect with it, can build a stronger, longer-lasting trust. It seems I've re-learned how to 'render' things and how it works with what people see."

The election results slowly trickled in, not with a bang, but with a steady, persistent wave. Sterling, the politician who was scared of pigeons and sometimes forgot his wife's name, was winning. By a small, but important, amount. People hadn't voted for a perfect, unreachable hologram, but for a tiny glimpse of someone who felt a little more like them, a little more human.

Jun Park, the ghostwriter who had once chased perfect falsehoods with all his might, found himself looking at his job with new, surprisingly hopeful eyes. And Mirror-7, the avatar that was always too honest, kept shining, a little less rigidly truthful, and a lot more wonderfully, vibrantly real. The world, it turned out, was ready for a little less polish and a lot more personality, even in the big, shimmering theatre of holographic politics. The cheers for Sterling, when they finally came, weren't just for a candidate, but for the imperfect, relatable human who had dared to be seen.
characters: Jun Park, professional ghostwriter for politicians' holograms; Mirror-7, an avatar renderer with too much honesty
